A common path starts with mechanical engineering or CNC study, followed by CNC operating experience. Learn CAD/CAM software, move into programming, and build process knowledge to become a senior programmer or process engineer.

This career suits people who enjoy mastering software and understand machining. Strong modelers with toolpath intuition who like working with the shop floor can connect digital design with physical production.

Computer Numerically Controlled Tool Programmers write and debug machining programs for CNC equipment. They build three-dimensional models from part drawings, design toolpaths, set machining parameters, verify programs in simulation, support trial cuts, and turn design intent into executable machining instructions.

paragraphs: The day follows a cycle of modeling, toolpath creation, simulation, and trial cutting. The morning goes to building a model from drawings and defining the fixture plan. In the afternoon, the programmer creates roughing and finishing toolpaths, sets speeds and feeds, verifies the simulation, and sends the program to the machine. If the trial part is out of tolerance, the programmer measures it on the shop floor, finds the cause, and revises parameters until it passes.

Employment is projected to reach 31,900 by 2034, a net increase of about 3,600 jobs, with about 3,100 openings per year. The 2026 median annual wage is about $65,700 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace Computer Numerically Controlled Tool Programmers, but it will remove much template-only work. CAM software with AI assistance can generate toolpaths for routine parts in seconds, reducing entry-level opportunities built on memorized settings. Process expertise remains valuable. People still decide how to fixture complex parts, choose tooling strategies, control deformation, and balance quality with throughput. Those judgments depend on shop-floor experience.

paragraphs: A score of 6/10 places this career in the moderate AI exposure range. Program generation has broad AI exposure, and automation now handles much routine work.

Moderate exposure does not mean the role disappears. AI replaces program generation, while process-design judgment becomes more valuable. Programmers who use AI tools and understand shop-floor processes can deliver much more, increasing their scarcity.

Study mechanical engineering, CNC machining, or intelligent manufacturing. Build strong CAD/CAM skills and learn machining processes. AI can replace routine programming, but not process judgment. Students need both capabilities.

Move beyond producing programs into multi-axis programming, difficult-part processes, and intelligent tool management. Use AI programming tools as assistants. Your value lies in judgment, not generation.

CNC operating experience creates a strong route into programming. Bring program samples and trial-cut improvement records to interviews. High-end manufacturers value proven work more than certificates alone.

Do not treat programmers as toolpath generators, because AI already handles much of that work. Hire versatile programmers who understand processes, work on the shop floor, and optimize plans with AI tools.
